title: Solutions to the diffusion equation applied to bacterial monolayers
text:
Abstract
This work presents several approaches to deriving analytical solutions to the diffusion equation on a 2D domain. We focus on cases common in modeling bacterial cell-cell signaling in monolayers, where cells secrete diffusible molecules that can be taken up by other cells or degraded in the environment. We start with simple cases of pure diffusion, then gradually add complexity by incorporating degradation, point sources, and sinks. We also compare the analytical solutions to numerical simulations to validate our results.

title: Part I
text:
This part shows cases in which analytical solutions exist. We start with the simplest case of pure diffusion, then add degradation, point sources, and finally discuss how to handle point sinks.
Chapters in this part:

Chapter 1 Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion with and without degradation
Chapter 2 Non-homogeneous case: adding point sources
Chapter 3 Effective solution: an approximation.
Chapter 4 Mixed boundary conditions

title: Homogeneous cases
text:
The initial and boundary conditions
Let’s find the analytical solution to the following diffusion equation:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 u
\tag{1}\]
The equation is defined on an two dimensional domain \(\Omega = [0,L_x] \times [0,L_y]\) (for example, a microfluidic chamber of size \(L_x\) by \(L_y\)) with reflective boundary conditions.
The initial condition \(u(x,y,t=0)\) is given by a set of \(N\) instantaneous point sources located at positions \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) with strengths \(\{S_i\}_{i=1}^N\): \[
u(x,y,0) = \sum_{i=1}^N S_i \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i)
\tag{2}\]
where \(\delta\) is the Dirac’s delta function.
The Neumann boundary conditions are given by: \[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=0} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=L_x} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=0} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=L_y} = 0
\tag{4}\]
The following sections are dedicated to finding the solution step by step, starting with the method of separation of variables. If interested in the final solution, you can jump to section Final solution.

title: Homogeneous cases
Homogeneous cases
Homogeneous cases
text:
Solving \(X(x)\) and \(Y(y)\)
Now let’s focus on finding the solution to equation Equation 1.4 and equation Equation 1.5.






NoteSolving the equation for X(x)





We want to find functions that, when doubly differentiated with respect to \(x\) , return the same function multiplied by a constant:
\[
\frac{d^2X}{dx^2} = -\lambda_x X
\]






NoteThis is an eigenvalue problem





We know that the double derivatives of exponential functions are proportional to the exponential function. So, let’s assume that the solution is an exponential function of the form \(X(x) = e^{kx}\), where \(k\) is an unknown constant. This way, if you take the second derivative of \(X(x)\), you will get:
\[
\frac{d^2X}{dx^2} = k^2 e^{kx}
\tag{1.7}\]
which would satisfy equation Equation 1.4 if \(k^2 = -\lambda_x\).
Additionally, since Equation 1.4 is a linear second-order ordinary differential equation, we also know that all its solutions can be expressed as a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions. These two independent solutions form a basis for the solution space:
\[
X(x) = C_1 X_1(x) + C_2 X_2(x)
\]



This leads us to a general solution of the form:
\[
X(x) = C_1 e^{k_1 x} + C_2 e^{k_2 x}
\tag{1.8}\]
where \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) are unknown constants.
Now we can solve for \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) depending on the sign of \(\lambda_x\):






NoteEvaluating different cases for λx






Positive \(\lambda_x\)






NoteEvaluating the case of positive λx





If \(\lambda_x > 0\), then \(k_1 = i\sqrt{\lambda_x}\) and \(k_2 = -i\sqrt{\lambda_x}\).
This means that the 2 independent solutions are:
\[
X_1(x) = e^{i\sqrt{\lambda_x} x}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
X_2(x) = e^{-i\sqrt{\lambda_x} x}
\]
Thus, the general solution is: \[
X(x) = C_1 e^{i\sqrt{\lambda_x} x} + C_2 e^{-i\sqrt{\lambda_x} x}
\] Using Euler’s formula \(e^{i\theta} = \cos(\theta) + i\sin(\theta)\), we can rewrite this as: \[
X(x) = A \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x) + B \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x)
\tag{1.9}\] Let’s now consider the boundary conditions shown in equation Equation 4.
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=0} = 0 \implies \frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} Y(y) T(t) = 0 \implies \frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = 0
\] This is because \(Y(y)\) and \(T(t)\) are not zero for all \(y\) and \(t\). If either of them were zero, then \(u(x,y,t)\) would be zero for all \(x\), which is not the case.
Calculating the derivative of Equation 1.9 gives:
\[
\frac{dX}{dx} = - A \sqrt{\lambda_x} \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x) + B \sqrt{\lambda_x} \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x)
\] Evaluating this at \(x=0\) gives:
\[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = B \sqrt{\lambda_x} = 0 \implies B = 0
\] Thus, the solution simplifies to: \[
X(x) = A \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x)
\] Now, applying the second boundary condition: \[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=L_x} = 0 \implies \frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = 0
\] Evaluating the derivative at \(x=L_x\) gives: \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = - A \sqrt{\lambda_x} \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} L_x) = 0
\] since \(A \neq 0\) and \(\sqrt{\lambda_x} \neq 0\), we have: \[
\sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} L_x) = 0 \implies \sqrt{\lambda_x} L_x = n \pi \implies \lambda_x = \frac{n^2 \pi^2}{L_x^2} \quad n \in \mathbb{Z^{>0}}
\]



If \(\lambda_x > 0\), then the solution to equation Equation 1.4 after applying the boundary conditions in Equation 4 is any eigenfunction of the form: \[
X_n(x) = A_n \cos\left(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x\right) \quad n \in \mathbb{Z^{>0}}
\] where \(A_n\) are arbitrary constants associated with each eigenvalue \(\lambda_x = \frac{n^2 \pi^2}{L_x^2}\).


Zero-valued \(\lambda_x\)






NoteEvaluating the case of zero λx





When \(\lambda_x = 0\), we get repeated roots \(k_1 = k_2 = 0\), this means that the general solution to equation Equation 1.4 is not given by a linear combination of two independent exponential functions.
Instead, we can substitute \(\lambda_x = 0\) into equation Equation 1.4, we get \(\frac{d^2X}{dx^2} = 0\). This is a simple second-order ordinary differential equation, and its general solution is a linear function of \(x\):
\[
X(x) = A + B x
\tag{1.10}\] where \(A\) and \(B\) are arbitrary constants that determine the specific solution depending on the boundary conditions. Applying the boundary conditions: \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = B = 0
\] and \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = B = 0
\]



If \(\lambda_x = 0\), then the solution to equation Equation 1.4 that satisfies the boundary conditions in Equation 4 is a constant \[
X(x) = A
\]


Negative \(\lambda_x\)






NoteEvaluating the case of negative λx





If \(\lambda_x < 0\), then \(k = \pm \sqrt{ |\lambda_x|}\). This means that the 2 independent solutions are:
\[
X_1(x) = e^{\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x}
\] and \[
X_2(x) = e^{-\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x}
\] which leads to the general solution: \[
X(x) = C_1 e^{\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x} + C_2 e^{-\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x}
\]
\[
X(x) = A \cosh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x) + B \sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x)
\tag{1.11}\]
The derivative of Equation 1.11 is: \[
\frac{dX}{dx} = A \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x) + B \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \cosh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x)
\]
Applying the first boundary condition:
\[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = B \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} = 0 \implies B = 0
\]
Thus, the solution simplifies to:
\[
X(x) = A \cosh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x)
\]
and applying the second boundary condition:
\[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = A \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} L_x) = 0
\]
Since \(A \neq 0\) and \(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \neq 0\), we have:
\[
\sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} L_x) = 0 \implies \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} L_x = 0 \implies \lambda_x = 0
\] This contradicts our initial assumption that \(\lambda_x < 0\).



Therefore, there are no solutions for \(\lambda_x < 0\).




This leads us to conclude that the only possible values for \(\lambda_x\) compatible with the boundary conditions in Equation 4 are \[
\lambda_x = \frac{n^2 \pi^2}{L_x^2} \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0},
\] where \(\mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}\) denotes the set of non‑negative integers. In particular, the case \(n = 0\) corresponds to the eigenvalue \(\lambda_x = 0\).



Thus, the general solution to equation Equation 1.4 that satisfies the boundary conditions in Equation 4 is:
\[
X_n(x) = A_n \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right), \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}.
\]
Similarly, the solution to equation Equation 1.5 that satisfies the boundary conditions in Equation 4 is:
\[
Y_m(y) = B_m \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right), \quad m \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}.
\]






NoteVisualizing the eigenfunctions Xn(x) and their second derivatives





To illustrate these eigenfunctions, we can plot \(X_n(x)\) and \(\frac{d²X_n}{dx^2}\) for different values of \(n\), \(A_n\), and \(L_x\):

In plot the plot above you can visualy confirm that the Equation 1.4 is satisfied for any \(X_n(x)\): when the eigenvalue \(\lambda_x\) is greater than 1, the double derivative \(\frac{d^2X_n}{dx^2}\) is just a scaled-up version of \(X_n(x)\) multiplied by \(-1\). On the other hand, when the eigenvalue \(\lambda_x\) is between 0 and 1, \(\frac{d^2X_n}{dx^2}\) is a scaled-down version of \(X_n(x)\) multiplied by \(-1\). In the graph above, you can also confirm that the zero-flux boundary conditions are satisfied for \(X_n(x)\) at \(x=0\) and \(x=L_x\) since the slope of \(X_n(x)\) is zero at these points.

title: Homogeneous cases
Homogeneous cases
section: Determining the amplitudes of the eigenmodes
text:
Determining the amplitudes of the eigenmodes
To find the constants \(C_{n,m}\), we can use the initial condition \(u(x,y,0)\). Evaluating the initial condition at \(t=0\) gives:
\[
u(x,y,0) =
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m} \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\tag{2.11}\]






NoteExpressing coefficients \(C_{n,m}\) in terms of the initial condition \(u(x,y,0)\)





We just need to find a way to calculate the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\). To do this, we will use the orthogonality property of the cosines to transform the infinite series problem into a integral calculation.
Let’s define a new set of eigenfunctions:
\[
\Phi_{p,q}(x,y) = \cos\left(\frac{p \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{q \pi}{L_y} y\right) \quad p,q \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}
\]
Now, we multiply both sides of equation Equation 2.11 by \(\Phi_{p,q}(x,y)\) to get:
\[
u(x,y,0) \Phi_{p,q}(x,y) =
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m} \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \Phi_{p,q}(x,y)
\tag{2.12}\]
Next, we integrate both sides of equation Equation 2.12 over the domain \(\Omega\):
\[
\int_{\Omega} u(x,y,0) \Phi_{p,q}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m} \int_{\Omega} \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \Phi_{p,q}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\tag{2.13}\]
As shown in Equation 2.9, the integral on the right-hand side of equation Equation 2.13 will be zero for all terms in the infinite sums except for the single term where \(n=p\) and \(m=q\).
Then, we can rewrite Equation 2.13 as:
\[
\int_{\Omega} u(x,y,0) \Phi_{p,q}(x,y) \, dy \, dx = C_{p,q} N_{x}(p) N_{y}(q)
\tag{2.14}\]
where
\[
N_{z}(r) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{L_z}{2} & \text{if } r > 0 \\
L_z & \text{if } r=0
\end{cases}
\]
Finally, we can solve for the coefficients \(C_{p,q}\):
\[
C_{p,q} = \frac{1}{N_{x}(p) N_{y}(q)} \int_{\Omega} u(x,y,0) \Phi_{p,q}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\tag{2.15}\]
But wait, we were looking for \(C_{n,m}\), not \(C_{p,q}\). However, since the only term that survived in the infinite sums was the one where \(n=p\) and \(m=q\), we can simply substitute \(p\) by \(n\) and \(q\) by \(m\), leading to the final expression for the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\):
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{1}{N_{x}(n) N_{y}(m)} \int_{\Omega} u(x,y,0) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\]



Thus, the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\) can be expressed as:
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \int_{\Omega} u(x,y,0) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\tag{2.16}\]
where
\[
\varepsilon_{q} =
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2} & \text{if } q=0 \\
1 & \text{if } q > 0
\end{cases}
\]
Now we can substitute the initial condition Equation 2 into equation Equation 2.16 to calculate the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\):
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \int_{\Omega} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N S_i \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i) \right) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\]






NoteSifting property of the Dirac delta function





Since the integral of the sum is equal to the sum of the integrals, we can rewrite this as:
\[C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N S_i \int_{\Omega} \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\]
Here we can use the sifting property of the Dirac delta function, which states that for any function \(f(x)\):
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}  \delta(x-a) f(x) \, dx = f(a)
\]
which tells us that the integral of a function multiplied by a Dirac delta function is just the value of the function at the point where the delta function is centered.
For our case, we have a product of two delta functions, \(\delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i)\), which means that the integral will pick out the value of \(\Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\) at the locations \((x_i,y_i)\) where the sources are located (e.g positions where cells released the chemical at time \(t=0\)):
\[
\int_{\Omega} \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \, dy \, dx = \Phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\]



Applying the sifting property of the Dirac delta function: \[
C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N S_i \Phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\tag{2.17}\]

title: Homogeneous cases
Non-homogeneous case
text:
Solution using eigenfunction expansion
Let’s now consider the non-homogeneous diffusion equation with a constant decay rate \(\beta\) and point-like sources that constantly inject material into the system:
\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 v + Q(x,y,t) - \beta v
  \tag{1}\]
where \[
Q(x,y,t) = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i(t) \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i)
\] represents point-like sources located at positions \((x_i,y_i)\) with time-dependent injection rates \(A_i(t) > 0\), and \(v(x,y,t)\) is the new function we want to solve for.
As before, we will assume reflective boundary conditions on all sides of the rectangular domain of size \(L_x \times L_y\)
We will start by assuming that the solution \(v(x,y,t)\) can be written as a sum of eigenmodes, similar to what we did in Equation 2.10 in Infinite sum of eigenmodes for the homogeneous case:
\[
v(x,y,t) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} T_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\tag{2}\]
where \(T_{n,m}(t)\) are time-dependent coefficients to be determined and \(\Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\) are the eigenfunctions of the Laplacian operator with Neumann boundary conditions (Equation 2.1).
We also express the source term \(Q(x,y,t)\) as a linear combination of the same eigenfunctions \(\Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\):
\[
Q(x,y,t)= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} q_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\tag{3}\]
where \(q_{n,m}(t)\) are the coefficients of the source term expansion, which can be determined by projecting \(Q(x,y,t)\) onto the eigenfunctions \(\Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\), as we will see later.
where \(q_{n,m}(t)\) are the coefficients of the source term expansion. To find these coefficients, we can use a similar procedure as the one described in Determining the amplitudes of the eigenmodes. But this time, instead of projecting the initial condition onto the eigenfunctions, we will project the time-dependent source term \(Q(x,y,t)\) onto the eigenfunctions:
This leads us to the following expression for \(q_{n,m}(t)\):
\[
q_{n,m}(t) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\tag{4}\]
Now we can substitute the expansion for \(v(x,y,t)\) and \(Q(x,y,t)\) into the original PDE Equation 1.
This leaves us with an ordinary differential equation for each mode \((n,m)\):
\[
\frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} + (D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta) T_{n,m}(t) = q_{n,m}(t)
\tag{5}\]
This is a first-order linear ODE, which we have to solve for each pair \((n,m)\)
Solving for \(T_{n,m}(t)\) gives:
\[
T_{n,m}(t) = e^{-k_{n,m} t}  T_{n,m}(0) + \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau
\]
We need to determine \(T_{n,m}(0)\) using the initial condition for \(v(x,y,0)\):
\[
v(x,y,0) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} T_{n,m}(0) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
Using the orthogonality property of the eigenfunctions shown in Infinite sum of eigenmodes, we can find \(T_{n,m}(0)\) as:
\[
T_{n,m}(0) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} v(x,y,0) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) dy dx
\tag{6}\]

title: Non-homogeneous case
text:
NoteDerivation of ODEs for eigenmode coefficients





Since the equation is large, we will represent the infinite sum of infinite eigenmodes as \(\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty}\) for brevity:
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \right) = D \nabla^2 \left( \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \right) +
\] \[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} q_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) - \beta \left( \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) \right)
\] Rearranging the terms gives:
\[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) = D \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \nabla^2 \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) +
\] \[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} q_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) - \beta \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
As shown in Eigenvalue equation verification, we know that the eigenfunctions \(\Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\) satisfy the eigenvalue equation shown in Equation 2.4. Which allows us to replace \(\nabla^2 \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\) with \(-\lambda_{n,m} \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\):
\[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) = -D \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \lambda_{n,m} T_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) +
\] \[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} q_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) - \beta \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
We can now group by the eigenfunctions \(\Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\):
\[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \left( \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} + (D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta) T_{n,m}(t) - q_{n,m}(t) \right) \Phi_{n,m}(x,y) = 0
\]
A linear combination of linearly independent eigenfunctions \(\Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\) can only be equal to zero if the coefficient of each eigenfunction is equal to zero.












NoteSolving the ODEs for eigenmode coefficients





For solving this, we can use the integrating Factor method, where we will use \(e^{k_{n,m} t}\) as the integrating factor, where \(k_{n,m} = D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta\).
Multiplying both sides of equation Equation 5 by the integrating factor gives:
\[
e^{k_{n,m} t} \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} + k_{n,m} e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) = q_{n,m}(t) e^{k_{n,m} t}
\]
The left-hand side can be recognized as the derivative of the product \(e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t)\):
\[
\frac{d}{dt} \left( e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) \right) = q_{n,m}(t) e^{k_{n,m} t}
\]
Integrating both sides with respect to \(t\) from \(0\) to \(t\) gives:
\[
\left[ e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) \right]_0^t = \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{k_{n,m} \tau} d\tau
\] This simplifies to: \[
e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) - T_{n,m}(0) = \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{k_{n,m} \tau} d\tau
\]

title: Non-homogeneous case
text:
Final solution
Substituting \(T_{n,m}(t)\) back into the eigenfunction expansion for \(v(x,y,t)\) in equation Equation 1.2, we obtain the final solution for the non-homogeneous diffusion equation with point-like sources:
\[
v(x,y,t) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \left[ e^{-k_{n,m} t}  T_{n,m}(0) + \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau \right] \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\] where
\[
k_{n,m} = D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta
\] \[
\lambda_{n,m} = \left( \frac{n \pi}{L_x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{m \pi}{L_y} \right)^2
\] \[
q_{n,m}(t) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i(t) \phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\] \[
T_{n,m}(0) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} v(x,y,0) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) dy dx
\]

title: Non-homogeneous case
text:
Steady-state solution
Let’s now evaluate the shape of the solution as \(t \to \infty\), which should correspond to the steady-state solution in which \(\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = 0\), assuming that the source terms \(A_i\) are constant in time.
As \(t \to \infty\), the exponential decay term \(e^{-k_{n,m} t}\) approaches zero for all modes \((n,m)\):
\[
\lim_{t \to \infty} e^{-k_{n,m} t} = 0
\]
Thus, the steady-state solution simplifies to:
\[
v_{ss}(x,y) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \left[ q_{n,m} \int_0^{t} e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau \right] \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\] Now let’s solve the integral:
\[
\int_0^{t}  e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau \] We can substitute \(u = t - \tau\), which gives \(d\tau = -du\). The limits of integration change accordingly: When \(\tau = 0\), \(u = t\); and when \(\tau = t\), \(u = 0\). Therefore, the integral becomes:
\[
\int_t^{0} e^{-k_{n,m} u} (-du) = \int_0^{t} e^{-k_{n,m} u} du = \left[ -\frac{1}{k_{n,m}} e^{-k_{n,m} u} \right]_0^{t} = \frac{1}{k_{n,m}} \left( 1 - e^{-k_{n,m} t} \right)
\]
Taking the limit as \(t \to \infty\), we find:
\[
\lim_{t \to \infty} \int_0^{t}  e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau = \frac{1}{k_{n,m}}
\]
Thus, the steady-state solution becomes:
\[
\boxed{
v_{ss}(x,y) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{q_{n,m}}{k_{n,m}} \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
}
\]
where \[
k_{n,m} = D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta
\] \[
\lambda_{n,m} = \left( \frac{n \pi}{L_x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{m \pi}{L_y} \right)^2
\] \[
q_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\] \[
\phi_{n,m} = \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right)
\]
We can confirm that this is the steady-state solution if we derive the solution directly from the steady-state version of the original PDE Equation 1, in which we set \(\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = 0\):
\[
0 = D \nabla^2 v_{ss} + Q(x,y) - \beta v_{ss}
\] Rearranging gives:
\[
D \nabla^2 v_{ss} - \beta v_{ss} = - Q(x,y)
\]
This is known as the inhomogeneous Helmholtz equation (also called the screened Poisson equation).

title: 1  Mixed boundary conditions
text:
1.1 Finding eigenfunctions with mixed boundary conditions
Let’s consider the same non-homogeneous diffusion equation described in Equation 1
\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 v + Q(x,y,t) - \beta v
\tag{1.1}\]
where \[
Q(x,y,t) = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i)
\] represents point-like sources located at positions \((x_i,y_i)\), with production rates \(A_i\). This time, we will impose mixed boundary conditions on one edge of the domain. This is with the goal of modeling the microfluidic device as a rectangular domain which has 3 impermeable walls (Neumann boundary conditions) and one edge that connects the chamber to an external reservoir, allowing for diffusion across the domain (Robin boundary condition).
For reflective (Neumann) boundaries: \[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=0} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=L_x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=0} = 0
\] For the Robin boundary at \(y=L_y\):
\[
-D \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=L_y} =J= k (v(x,L_y,t) - v_{ext})
\]
\(J\) is the diffusion flux across the Robin boundary in the outward normal direction, and it is proportional to the concentration difference between the interior part of the domain at \(y=L_y\) and an external reservoir with concentration \(v_{ext}\), \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient, \(k\) is the mass transfer coefficient. For simplicity, we will assume that \(v_{ext}\) is zero.
Let’s solve this equation using 2 different methods: Eigenfunction expansion and Green’s functions.
But first, we need to find the eigenfunctions that satisfy the mixed boundary conditions.
To find the eigenfunctions, we start with the spatial eigenvalue problem associated with the homogeneous part of the diffusion equation:
\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 v - \beta v
\tag{1.2}\] We assume that the solution can be separated into spatial and temporal parts:
\[
v(x,y,t) = X(x) Y(y) T(t)
\]
Substituting this into Equation 1.2 gives:
\[
XY \frac{dT}{dt} = D T \left( Y \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + X \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} \right) - \beta XYT
\] Dividing both sides by \(XYTD\) leads to:
\[
\frac{1}{D T} \frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} - \frac{\beta}{D}
\] reorganizing terms, we have: \[
\frac{1}{D T} \frac{dT}{dt} + \frac{\beta}{D} = \frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2}
\]
since the left side depends only on time and the right side only on space, both sides must equal a constant, which we denote as \(-\lambda\). This gives us two separate equations:
\[
\frac{1}{D T} \frac{dT}{dt} + \frac{\beta}{D} = -\lambda
\] \[
\frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} = -\lambda
\] This gives us 3 ordinary differential equations:
\[\frac{dT}{dt} = -(\lambda + \frac{\beta}{D}) DT \tag{1.3}\] \[\frac{d^2X}{dx^2} = -\lambda_x X \tag{1.4}\] \[\frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} = -\lambda_y Y \tag{1.5}\] with the constraint that \(\lambda = \lambda_x + \lambda_y\).
The solution to Equation 1.3 is:
\[
T(t) = T(0) e^{-(\lambda + \frac{\beta}{D}) Dt}
\]
Next, we need to solve Equation 1.4 and Equation 1.5. As shown in Section 1.2.1, the general solutions are:
\[
X(x) = A_x \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x) + B_x \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x)
\] \[
Y(y) = A_y \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_y} y) + B_y \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_y} y)
\]
Let’s apply the boundary conditions to find the constants and the allowed values of \(\lambda_x\) and \(\lambda_y\).
For the Neumann boundary conditions at \(x=0\) and \(x=L_x\): \[
\frac{dXYT}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = YT \frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = 0
\] \(Y\) and \(T\) can not be zero for all \(y\) and \(t\), so we have: \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = 0 \implies B_x = 0
\] Next, we apply the Neumann boundary condition at \(x=L_x\): \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = 0 \implies -A_x \sqrt{\lambda_x} \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} L_x) = 0
\] This leads to the allowed values of \(\lambda_x\): \[\sqrt{\lambda_x} L_x = n \pi \implies \lambda_x = \left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x}\right)^2, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}\]
Thus, the eigenfunctions in the \(x\) direction are: \[\boxed{
X_n(x) = A_n \cos\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L_x}\right)}\]
Now, let’s apply the reflective boundary condition at \(y=0\): \[
\frac{dY}{dy}\Big|_{y=0} = 0 \implies B_y = 0
\]
Next, we apply the Robin boundary condition at \(y=L_y\):
\[
-D \frac{d YXT}{dy}\Big|_{y=L_y} = k (Y(L_y)XT - v_{ext})
\]
We will assume \(v_{ext}=0\). Dividing both sides by \(XT\), we get:
\[
-D \frac{dY}{dy}\Big|_{y=L_y} = k (Y(L_y))
\] Substituting the expression for \(Y(y)\), we have: \[
-D \left(-A_y \sqrt{\lambda_y} \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_y} L_y)\right) = k \left(A_y \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_y} L_y)\right)
\] Rearranging terms, we obtain the following equation: \[ \tan(\sqrt{\lambda_y} L_y) = \frac{k}{D \sqrt{\lambda_y}} \]
Let’s plot the left and right sides of this equation to find the allowed values of \(\lambda_y\).
Code
Plotly = require("plotly.js-dist@2")

k = 10
D = 1
Ly = 1

x = Array.from({length: 2000}, (_, i) => (i + 1) * 0.005) // avoid xi=0

// Tune these:
YMAX = 10          // don’t draw tan outside [-YMAX, YMAX]
COS_EPS = 1e-3     // don’t draw near asymptotes where cos≈0
pointsX = [1.43, 4.315, 7.25]
pointsY = pointsX.map(xi => k / (D * xi))
y1 = x.map(xi => {
  const u = xi * Ly
  const c = Math.cos(u)
  if (Math.abs(c) < COS_EPS) return null     // break line near asymptotes
  const t = Math.tan(u)
  if (!Number.isFinite(t)) return null
  if (Math.abs(t) > YMAX) return null        // optional: also clip large values
  return t
})

y2 = x.map(xi => k / (D * xi)) // this has a singularity at 0; x starts > 0

plot = {
  const div = document.createElement("div")
  div.style.height = "400px"
  div.style.width = "600px"

  Plotly.newPlot(div, [
    {x, y: y1, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "tan(√λy * Ly)"},
    {x, y: y2, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "k / (D * √λy)"},
    {
      x: pointsX,
      y: pointsY,
      type: "scatter",
      mode: "markers",
      name: "solutions",
      marker: {color: "red", size: 8}
    }
  ], {
    title: "Finding Eigenvalues λy",
    xaxis: {title: "√λy"},
    yaxis: {title: "Value", range: [-1, 10]},
    width: 600,
    height: 400,
    margin: {l: 20, r: 0, b: 30, t: 30}
  })

  return div
}
